VIABILITY: The model has real early evidence. Four paid pilots totaling $41,500 against roughly $12,000 in expenses is meaningful traction for a student venture, and the interview base (31 leaders) supports a genuine pain point. The revenue mechanics are clear: annual contracts at $18,000, installment payments, a lighter $9,500 entry tier, and $2,500 add-ons create a plausible land-and-expand path. Pricing sits well between per-student software and $50K+ consultancies. However, 'profitable on paper' is misleading because founders take no salary and coach time is unpaid or underpriced; true unit economics are unproven. The 60% gross margin is an unverified claim given that delivery is human-intensive.

SCALABILITY: This is the central weakness. The core differentiator, a human coach sitting with teachers, is labor-bound. Each school requires three cycles, three workshops per cycle (about nine workshops), three briefs, and an impact report. At 60 schools, that is hundreds of on-site or live sessions per year, which requires a sizable coaching staff with travel, quality control, and turnover. The plan to hire two part-time coaches does not match the projection of 12 schools next year, let alone 30 and 60. The claim that margins will rise from templates and dashboards is plausible but undemonstrated, and automating the coaching element undermines the very differentiation being sold. It is a services business with software leverage at the margins, so expect services-style growth (linear, margin-constrained), not software-style scaling. Geographic spread also raises travel costs and dilutes the 'relationships' advantage.

ASSUMPTION VALIDITY: (1) TAM of $63M assumes 3,500 schools all paying $18K; this is a ceiling, not a market, and ignores budget constraints at small charters (an $18K line item is significant when per-pupil funding is tight and Title/ESSER-type funds are shrinking). (2) The 'need only 3% share' framing is a common fallacy; the real question is conversion and sales-cycle length. (3) Projections of 12, 30, and 60 schools (roughly 2.5x then 2x growth) rest on four pilots, only two of which expressed intent to renew (not signed). Pilots at presumably discounted or partial scope are not equivalent to full $18K contracts; the average revenue per pilot (about $10,400) is well below the planned price, suggesting price realization risk. (4) Conversations with 30+ leaders in-state are not pipeline; no conversion rate, sales cycle length, or CAC is provided. School sales are slow, seasonal (budget cycles, spring/summer decisions), and relationship-driven. (5) Break-even 'by mid year two' is asserted without a cost model. (6) The business depends on measurable student growth to drive renewals; attribution is hard, results can be noisy over a short window, and a failed outcome in a small sample could hurt renewals and word of mouth. (7) The competitive moat is thin: the approach is replicable by any consulting firm or by software vendors adding coaching, and templates are not proprietary. Advisors' unpaid time and student-team availability also create key-person and continuity risks (graduation, part-time capacity).

VERDICT: A credible, customer-validated niche service with a clear route to revenue and a sensible price point, likely viable as a small, profitable consultancy. Venture-scale growth is doubtful without a deliberate shift toward leverage (train-the-trainer, coach-certification, software-enabled self-service, or district/network licensing). Priorities: convert pilots to signed annual contracts, document true delivery hours per school and fully loaded margin, build a pipeline with conversion data, and test a lower-touch tier that can scale beyond founder time.

Business plan text:

Graderoom Insight
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Graderoom Insight LLC
Overview
Graderoom Insight is a student founded consulting and training company that help small charter schools turn assessment data into targeted lesson plans. We are a registered LLC out of our university and we have paying customers already. This summary is going to explain the problem, our solution, the market, how we make money, who we compete with, our team, where we are at, and what we are asking for in this competition.
The Problem
Charter schools in the United States have alot of pressure to show results, and they give many assessments every year, interim tests, benchmark tests, state tests and so on. Big districts have whole offices of data analysts and instructional coaches. Small charter schools, which we define as one to three campuses with under 600 students, do not have this. Usually the principal is also the data person, or a teacher gets extra duties to look at scores for a stipend. What we heard again and again in our interviews with 31 school leaders and teachers over the last year is that data comes in and nothing happens with it. One principal told us the test reports are 'a pile on my desk I feel bad about.' Teachers told us they get a score report weeks after testing and it tells them a student is 'below basic' but not WHAT to teach on Monday. The gap is not data, the gap is turning data into action in the classroom. When this gap exists, students who are behind stay behind, and schools risk their charter renewals because renewal depends on growth numbers. This is a real and expensive problem for the schools and for the kids.
Our Solution
Graderoom Insight provides a full cycle service. First, we take in the schools assessment exports, whatever format they have. Second, our team analyzes the results at the standard level, the class level and the student group level, and we produce a short plain language findings brief, no more than two pages, so busy leaders will actually read it. Third, and this is what makes us different, we run a coaching session with the teachers where we convert the findings into actual lesson plans, small group rosters and reteach activities for the next two to three weeks. Fourth, we come back after the next assessment and measure if the students actually moved on the targeted standards, so the loop is closed. Our MVP includes a simple dashboard we built and a library of lesson plan templates tied to standards. Most competitors sell software or sell generic professional development. We sell the bridge between the two, with a human coach who sits with the teachers, supported by our tools.
Market
There are roughly 8,000 charter schools in the country, and a big share of them are small independent ones that are not part of large networks with central offices. We estimate about 3,500 schools fit our target profile. If each pays an average of 18,000 dollars per year, the total addressable market is around 63 million dollars annually for just this segment. We do not need to capture much of this to have a real business. Winning 100 schools, under 3 percent of the target group, would be 1.8 million dollars in yearly revenue. We are starting in our home state where there are about 140 small charters, and we have already talked to leaders at over 30 of them. Charter school leaders also talk to each other thru associations and conferences, so word of mouth can spread fast in this market.
Business Model
We sell an annual partnership package to each school. The standard package is 18,000 dollars per year and includes three data cycles, three teacher coaching workshops per cycle, a findings brief for each cycle, access to our dashboard and templates, and one end of year impact report. We also offer a lighter package at 9,500 dollars for single cycle support, and add on one time workshops at 2,500 dollars each. Our costs are mostly coach time, so our gross margin is about 60 percent at current delivery costs, and we expect it to rise as our templates and dashboard reduce prep time per school. Schools pay in two installments, which helps our cash flow. Renewals are the key to the model, and our impact reports are designed to show growth so schools see the value and sign again.
Competition
Our competition falls into three groups. The first is assessment and analytics software companies, which sell dashboards but leave the schools to figure out what to do with them, and their prices are per student which gets expensive for small schools that also have to train staff. The second is large education consulting firms, who are very expensive, often 50,000 dollars or more, and focus on big districts. The third is doing nothing or doing it in house, which is what most small charters do now. Our advantage is that we are priced for small schools, we focus only on this segment, and we deliver the last step, the lesson plans, that others skip. We are aware that a bigger firm could copy our approach, but our early relationships and our templates give us a head start.
Team
Marisol Tevanian is CEO and leads sales and school relationships. She is a senior studying education policy and worked two years as a tutor and aide in a charter school. Dwight Okonkwo-Hale is our head of analytics, a statistics major who built the dashboard prototype and does all the data work. Priyanka Lindqvist leads coaching and curriculum, she is a graduate student in teaching and learning with three years of classroom experience as a middle school math teacher. We also have two advisors, a retired charter school principal and a faculty member who studies assessment, who both give us time for free.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined the core concept, built a working prototype, registered our LLC, launched a website, and gotten our first outside users. Four charter schools have paid for pilots, for total revenue of 41,500 dollars over the last two semesters. Of these, two have already said they want to sign the full annual package next year. Our expenses so far were about 12,000 dollars, mostly travel, software and legal fees for the LLC, so we are profitable on paper, although the founders have not taken salaries. For next year we project 12 schools and about 190,000 dollars in revenue, 30 schools and 520,000 dollars in year two, and 60 schools and over 1 million dollars in year three. We project to break even on hiring costs by the middle of year two.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for the competition prize money, which we would use mainly to hire two part time coaches who are former teachers, improve the dashboard so it can take more file formats automatically, and pay for travel to the charter school conferences where we can find new customers. We would also welcome mentors with experience in selling to schools and in building services companies that are able to scale. With support from this competition we believe we can double our customers within one year and become the go to partner for small charter schools who want their data to actually help kids learn.
Thank you for considering Graderoom Insight.

Question: Comment on the viability and scalability of the business model and strategy. Address whether the company has a clear path to making money and growing, and evaluate the validity of the entrepreneur's assumptions.
